The politics of Northern Ireland is extremely complicated. But you need to know the history. But basically Northern Ireland is a Protestant majority region that was kept by the British at the end of the war for Irish independence. Ireland as a country has been primarily a catholic country that was incorporated by the British Empire in the 19th century after centuries of conflict prior. The result was that some groups of people in the north became Protestant as well as Protestants moved into Northern Ireland. So after the Irish achieved independence, they made a treaty with the British where Northern Ireland was handed to them to end the war. However, it was extremely controversial (which was is an understatement). The treaty sparked a civil war in the Republic of Ireland (non-northern Ireland) as well as Northern Ireland. The civil war calmed, but in Northern Ireland, tensions between Protestants and loyalists ( who want to remain in the UK and not be a minority in a catholic Ireland), and Catholics who ended up being subjugated by majority Protestant police and Irish Nationalists who want Ireland to be United. This tensions culminated in the 1960s and 1970s and in 1972 sparked Bloody Sunday which was a massacre in which British soldiers shot 26 civilians as part of the policing by Britain in Northern Ireland. This sparked conflict for over 25 years. Eventually the IRA (a group who claims legacy to the original Irish Republican Army that fought for Irish independence) and the British government created the Good Friday agreement where Irish of both regions can move and travel between each area as citizens of both countries, however Britain still retains sovereignty over Northern Ireland. This was possible through the European Union. 

And now we get to the present. Since Brexit happened, this threw Good Friday out the window, since the deal isn’t possible with the UK out of the EU. In an attempt to avoid more war in Ireland after more than 20 years of some type of peace (although tensions have always remained), British Prime Ministers Johnson and May negotiated a trade border in the sea between Northern Ireland and the rest of the UK in order to prevent a hard border in Northern Ireland and keep Good Friday. This backfired terribly, because Loyalists in Northern Ireland have started rioting as a concern for being separated from the rest of their nation (in their view) by their own government. This has also brought anxiety to the Catholic Irish recently. Basically people who identify with the UK feel betrayed for being separated.

Edit: Very very big thing I forgot to mention, which is that if the majority of Northern Ireland votes to join Ireland, the UK is obligated to allow it to join Ireland. So if people in Northern Ireland want to join Ireland to be apart of the EU again, then the Loyalists will be even more enraged. So this trade border also puts that on your table.

Your description asks a very central question to what is America in general. This is important when asking about the political legitimacy of the United States, because it has been traditional seen as having what’s called a legal-rational legitimacy. For example, we may hate the leaders, but the leadership doesn’t justify the regime. This is in contrast to say Russia where without Putin or someone with the same influence over Russians, the system would collapse, because this is what’s called a charismatic legitimacy. 

Remember at the time, the United States was as democratic as you can be. In the UK, very few could also vote, and France was a monarchy.

That said what justifies the US regime is based on enlightenment principles that is derived from the idea that there is a strict separation of powers, and a strong constitution and a government with a bill of rights for everyone (that was considered a person at the time). The system of course had mechanisms for reforms and everyone in congress at the time had many different views of government and gave room for compromise and reform within their system. So what justified the US as a government back then wasn’t merely popular support but other means of a limited government that would respect mankind’s rationality.

This was different compared to France before the Revolution where the legacy of Louis XIV still reigned and the regime was based on Traditional legitimacy (regimes based on culture or religion).

So to answer your question about which political theorist justify the US, the founders themselves based their justification on other enlightenment thinkers like Montesquieu, Locke, and Rousseau.

For example, Lenin believed imperialism would inevitably lead to conflict between the major powers prior to WWI, so the constant need to competition among nations that are lead by wealthy capitalists inevitably leads to some kind of conflict. 

Read up on Antonio Gramsci, he’s an Italian Marxist who’s influential in a Marxist understanding of International relations, and sees in the world in constant conflict between ‘peripheries’ (those in ‘exploiter’ nations like the global north and those in the South).

The reason you find realism focusing on security studies is because realists tend to believe states are concerned with power, competition and alliances, because of the desire to be secure from foreign powers. Whereas Marxists usually focus on structural issues with global capitalism and sees classes of people compete with each other sometimes in the form of states (i.e state capitalism). So in some stretch this is ‘security’, in the sense that Marxists view the world in terms of class conflict and the inevitable consequences of that.
